# Incident Handling Document — `ledger-reconcile` Failed on Three Consecutive Nights

**Prepared:** 2026-08-09 · **Audience:** the on-shift engineer who holds this at the moment the third failure is recognised · **Status:** follow as written

---

## 1. What this document covers

The nightly `ledger-reconcile` job has failed on three consecutive nights. This is the case the job runbook names explicitly, and it is not a judgement call: **failures on three consecutive nights open a severity band B incident.** The reasoning recorded in the runbook is that at three nights the reconciliation has not been proved for a full accounting period, and the question is no longer whether the job runs.

Two distinctions govern everything below, and getting them wrong is the recorded reason most overnight pages reach the wrong person:

- **Failing is not reporting.** A job *fails* when it cannot complete. A job *reports a problem* when it completes and dislikes what it saw. This incident is a failure of the job, not a set of breaks.
- **A break is not a failure.** A break is one discrepancy the reconciliation writes between the settled-invoice view and the ledger extract. Breaks are expected in small numbers and are worked the next morning under the break triage guide. They are not what this incident is about, though breaks produced by any manual run you do during the incident are still worked normally.

**How this is normally recognised.** The overnight failure review reads three nights at a time, not one, precisely so that a repeat is visible. A job failing once is noise; the same job failing across consecutive nights is what the review exists to notice. If you are the on-shift engineer and the third failure has just landed in front of you, the trigger has fired regardless of whether the morning review has run yet — anyone may open an incident, and the bias toward opening one is deliberate.

---

## 2. Open the incident — do this first

Open the incident before you diagnose anything. Opening one costs almost nothing; not opening one costs the timeline, which is the part hardest to reconstruct later.

**What the record needs at the moment of opening:**

| Field | What goes in it |
| --- | --- |
| One-line statement of what is wrong | e.g. "`ledger-reconcile` has failed on three consecutive scheduled runs; the reconciliation is unproved for those business dates." |
| The system it is wrong in | The nightly `ledger-reconcile` job, reconciliation window 04:00–05:30. |
| Who opened it | You, by name. |
| Severity band | **Band B.** |

Everything else is filled in as it is learned. Do not hold the incident open-pending while you gather a complete picture — an incident that waits for a complete picture before it exists has no early timeline.

**Do not write a cause into the opening record.** At this point nobody knows it, and a guess in an opening record outlives the incident.

**Note the clock start time to the minute.** Every escalation clock below runs from this moment.

### Why band B, and not another band

The bands are a statement about consequence, not effort:

- **Band A** is customer-visible loss of service, or a defect that has *already produced an incorrect external figure*.
- **Band B** is an internal control that has stopped proving what it exists to prove, with **no external figure yet affected**. This is exactly the state of a reconciliation that has not run.
- **Band C** is a degradation with a known workaround already in place.
- **Band D** is a defect with no consequence before the next working day.

**Band B is the floor here, not the ceiling.** If at any point you establish that an incorrect external figure has already gone out — for example, that something downstream consumed partial or unreconciled input and a figure left the platform on it — the consequence has changed and the incident is band A, which follows the red route with far shorter clocks. The overnight failure review flags "whether anything downstream ran on partial input" specifically because a job that succeeded on incomplete input leaves no failure record anywhere. Check this deliberately; it will not announce itself.

---

## 3. Who has to be told

Band B notification, as the severity standard sets it:

1. **The owning team of the job.**
2. **The platform group's shift lead.**

Band B is *not* notified to the whole platform group; that is band A's rule. Do not broadcast wider than the standard sets, and do not narrow it either.

> **Gap — the material is silent on this.** Nothing in the available material names the owning team for `ledger-reconcile`. The runbook, the failure history and the escalation pages all refer to "the owning team" without identifying it for this job. Resolve this from the roster before you page, and record in the incident who you identified and how. Do not guess an owner from the job's subject matter.

The shift lead is also the first rung of the escalation route, so the notification and the first escalation step are the same action here.

---

## 4. Escalation — the amber route and its clocks

Band B follows the **amber route**.

### The rungs

| Rung | Who | Reached on (primary) | Fallback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First | The owning team's shift lead | Pager app | Phone |
| Second | The platform duty manager | Phone | Pager app |
| Third | The head of platform | Phone | The assistant's phone |

An incident occupies exactly one rung at a time, and climbs one rung at a time. **Skipping a rung is allowed only when the person on that rung is the one escalating** — so if you are the shift lead, you may go straight to the duty manager.

The amber route has three rungs. The executive on call sits on the red route only and is not part of this escalation.

### The clocks

Each figure is the longest the incident may sit on that rung before it must reach the next one:

| Route | First rung | Second rung | Third rung |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Amber (this incident)** | **20 minutes** | **25 minutes** | **2 hours** |
| Red (for reference) | 5 minutes | 10 minutes | 30 minutes |
| Standard (for reference) | 4 hours | next working day | next working day |

Three rules attach to these clocks, and all three matter tonight:

- **A clock starts when the incident is opened, not when it is acknowledged.** Silence from the rung does not pause anything.
- **Clocks run across shift handovers.** A handover does not reset or suspend them.
- **An unacknowledged clock that expires climbs on its own.** The escalation is automatic. You do not hold the climb back waiting for the acknowledgement — the acknowledgement is recorded late instead.

> **Ambiguity you must resolve locally — flagging it rather than papering over it.** The response matrix states both that each figure is a per-rung hold time *and* that "a clock starts when the incident is opened." Those two statements give different schedules for the second and third climbs, and the material does not disambiguate them:
>
> | Reading | Reaches duty manager | Reaches head of platform |
> | --- | --- | --- |
> | All clocks run from open (the literal text) | T+20 min | T+25 min |
> | Each clock runs from arrival on its rung | T+20 min | T+45 min |
>
> **Escalate on the earlier of the two.** Under band B the cost of climbing early is a woken manager; the cost of climbing late is an unproved control sitting still. Record which reading you applied in the incident record so the reviewer can see it, and raise the ambiguity as a correction candidate in the postmortem.

### Overnight — the doubling does *not* apply here

Between 22:00 and 06:00 the **standard route's** clocks are doubled, because the rung below it is on a pager rather than at a desk. **The red and amber routes are worked to the same clocks at every hour.** A three-night reconcile failure is recognised at or shortly after the end of the 04:00–05:30 reconciliation window — inside the 22:00–06:00 band — and the twenty-minute first-rung clock still applies in full. The stated reasoning: an incident on either of those routes is already past the point where the hour is an excuse.

### When a page is not answered

Paging behaviour is per role, not per incident:

- A page unacknowledged on the **primary** channel within its own window repeats on the **fallback**.
- A page unacknowledged on **both** means that person is treated as unreachable. **The sender moves on rather than waiting** — which, combined with the automatic climb, means an unreachable rung does not stall the incident.
- A channel change made mid-incident does not silently redirect a page already in flight; directory changes take effect on the next shift.

> **Gap — the material is silent on this.** The paging directory says a page repeats on the fallback "within its own window" but nowhere states the length of that window for any role. You therefore cannot compute the repeat time from the material. Use the escalation clock as the binding constraint: whatever the repeat window is, the incident must have *reached* the next rung by the figure in the matrix. If the fallback attempt has not been acknowledged by the time the rung's clock expires, climb.

### Who is actually on each rung tonight

- **Shift lead / on-call engineer:** the platform rotation runs week-long shifts handed over on Tuesday mornings. **The roster is the source of truth, not the conversation that preceded it** — an unrecorded swap is the most common recorded reason a page reaches the wrong person. Read the roster; do not page from memory.
- **Duty manager:** the role rotates monthly among the platform leads, published a quarter ahead. If the holder named a standing delegate for this window, **the delegate holds the role**, not assists in it — there is never a state with two holders or none. A rota correction made less than a day ahead is announced in the platform channel as well as recorded, so check the channel as well as the rota.
- **The morning batch review engineer is not a pager rung.** The review shift is a daytime duty and carries no pager. Do not escalate to them; the review is a reading, not a repair, and anything needing repair is handed to the owning team.

### Every climb is written down

Each climb writes a line to the incident record containing: **the rung it left, the rung it reached, the clock that expired, and whether it expired unacknowledged.** Write these as they happen, not retrospectively.

> **Gap — the material is silent on this.** The amber route ends at the head of platform, and the matrix gives that third rung a two-hour clock — but amber has no fourth rung for it to climb to, and nothing in the material says what happens when that two-hour clock expires. If the incident is still unheld at that point, escalate by judgement (the red route's fourth rung is the executive on call) and record explicitly that you went outside the defined route and why. Do not let the incident sit silently on an exhausted route.

---

## 5. What is communicated while it is open

### The opening notice

It says three things, and stops:

1. **What is affected** — the nightly reconciliation has not run for the affected business dates; those dates are unproved against the ledger.
2. **What is not affected** — state this positively and only for what you have actually checked. Do not assert that nothing downstream is affected until you have checked whether anything ran on partial input.
3. **When the next update will come.**

**It does not say what the cause is.** Nobody knows it yet, and a guess in an opening notice outlives the incident.

### The rhythm of updates

Updates go out on the cadence the opening notice promised — **including the updates that say nothing has changed.** A silent incident is read as a resolved one.

> **Gap — the material is silent on this.** No standard update interval is defined for any band. The cadence is whatever your opening notice commits to, so commit to one explicitly and then keep it. Pick an interval you can actually hold overnight, and if the incident quiets down, say so on schedule rather than going quiet.

### Who speaks outside the platform group

**Only the incident lead.** The recorded reason is not secrecy: two well-meaning people describing the same partial picture produce three versions of it. If finance, the upstream file's owners, or anyone else outside the platform group needs to be told something, it goes through the lead.

> **Gap — the material is silent on this.** Nothing available defines who the incident lead is for a band B incident, or how the role is assigned. Name a lead explicitly when you open the incident, record the name, and re-record it if it changes at a handover — otherwise the "only the lead speaks outward" rule has no referent.

### Language

Avoid **"should be fixed"**, **"briefly"**, and **"minor"**. Say what was observed and what was done. This applies to the incident record as much as to the notices.

---

## 6. Working the incident

The escalation and communication obligations above run on their own clocks and do not wait for the diagnosis. Do the following in parallel with them.

### 6.1 Establish which input is missing

The job fails when it cannot read one of its two inputs — the settled-invoice view or the general ledger extract — and the usual reason is that the ledger extract has not landed. Check the extract first, and **check the manifest before the file**:

| What you find | What it means | Where it goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manifest present, file absent | The transfer failed | Upstream transfer owners |
| No manifest at all | The upstream job did not run | Upstream finance system owners |
| File present, row count below the manifest | Truncated — it is quarantined rather than loaded | Upstream, with the quarantine record |
| Manifest row count and checksum both match | The extract is delivered; the failure is elsewhere | Owning team |

The extract is not considered delivered until **both** the row count and the checksum match. A truncated extract that gets loaded looks exactly like a night on which finance posted very little, and the difference surfaces only a period later — this is why quarantine exists and why you do not force a load past it.

> **Gap — the material is silent on this.** The extract runbook states that the manifest-without-file case and the no-manifest-at-all case "go to different people," but does not name either party. Identify them from the roster or from the upstream contact record, and write down in the incident who you contacted.

### 6.2 Check the timing before concluding the extract is late

- The extract is due **nightly at 03:40**, and **by 06:00 on the first two working days of a month**, when the close batch runs ahead of it.
- The reconciliation window is **04:00–05:30**.
- **These two facts conflict on the first two working days of a month.** On those nights the extract may be legitimately due as late as 06:00, after the reconciliation window has already closed. If the affected nights fall in that span, the job's failure may be a scheduling consequence rather than an upstream fault, and the correction belongs in the calendar rather than the job. Check the dates of the three failed nights against the close calendar before you attribute a cause.
- A job that overruns its window is not killed, but the window behind it starts late and the delay accumulates across the night. If an earlier window overran, reconciliation may have started late or against an input that was not yet in place — the ordered windows are collector drain (22:00–23:15), raw exports (23:15–00:45), maintenance and vacuum (00:45–02:00), aggregation (02:00–04:00), reconciliation (04:00–05:30).

### 6.3 Read the failure history against tonight

Eleven failures in two years, grouped into three causes:

- **Late extract** — by far the most common; the upstream file had not landed when the job started. **Every one of these cleared on the next schedule.** Three consecutive nights is therefore *not* this pattern, which is itself diagnostic.
- **Schema drift** — the extract gained a column and the loader rejected the file. Two occurrences, **both after an upstream release.** Ask whether there has been an upstream release in the last three days.
- **Consecutive failures** — one prior occurrence, on exactly three consecutive nights, caused by **a transfer credential that had expired** and was renewed only after the third morning. That occurrence is the reason the consecutive-failure case is now handled explicitly rather than as three unrelated single failures. **Check credential and certificate expiry on the transfer path early.** It is the one recorded precedent that matches this shape.

The history is explicit that none of it substitutes for the current night's run log. Read the log.

### 6.4 Manual runs — what they do and do not do

Once a missing input has landed, the reconciliation can be run by hand against a named business date:

- A manual run takes **one business date and both of that date's inputs**. It **refuses to start if either input is absent** — the same refusal the scheduled run makes, for the same reason: a reconciliation against one side is not a reconciliation. Do not attempt to work around this refusal.
- Run it from the platform host with the date, **wait for the break count, and read the breaks rather than the exit code.**
- **An enormous break count almost always means the extract was for a different date.** Stop and check the date before treating those breaks as real.
- Work any resulting breaks under the triage guide: **timing** breaks self-clear on the next run and are worth investigating only when the same key breaks on three separate nights; **sign** breaks (magnitude agrees, direction disagrees — almost always a refund recorded upstream as a charge) do not self-clear; **orphan** breaks older than one close period stop being a data question and become an accounting one, handed to finance with the record rather than resolved in the platform.

**A manual run settles the numbers for that date. It does not settle whether the scheduled job is healthy, it is not evidence that the next night will run, and it does not clear the open incident.** Run one per affected business date anyway — that is how the unproved dates get proved — but do not let a successful manual run change the incident's state.

### 6.5 Changes during a close freeze

Platform changes touching anything the ledger reads are frozen from the last working day of the month to the second working day of the next. **The freeze does not stop an incident response**, and a change applied during a freeze for incident reasons is recorded as such. Check the calendar for the current date; on 2026-08-09 the July/August freeze window has already passed, but check rather than assume, and if you are inside one, apply the change and record the freeze exception explicitly.

Corrections inside a closed period are never restated in place — a correction is posted into the open period with a reference back. If the affected business dates fall inside a closed period, that is a finance-side constraint, and it goes to finance with the record.

---

## 7. What has to be true before it can be closed

**Closing needs evidence that the condition has gone, not an absence of further reports.** For a scheduled job, that means **a clean scheduled run**.

Concretely, all of the following must hold:

1. **The scheduled `ledger-reconcile` run has completed cleanly in its own 04:00–05:30 window**, on the schedule, without intervention. The runbook is explicit: the incident closes on the evidence that the *scheduled* run has recovered, not on a successful manual one.
2. **Every business date that went unreconciled has been reconciled** — by manual run, per business date, with both inputs present, and with the break count read rather than the exit code.
3. **The breaks those runs produced have been handed to their proper destination** under the triage guide (sign breaks and old orphans do not self-clear and do not resolve by waiting).
4. **The downstream question has been answered**: whether anything ran on partial or unreconciled input, and if so what was done about it. If something did and a figure left the platform, the band was wrong and that must be reflected before closing.
5. **The escalation record is complete** — every climb has its line, including any that expired unacknowledged.

The earliest possible closure is therefore **after the next scheduled night's run**, not on the day the fix is applied. That is a design property of the rule, not a delay to be optimised away.

**An incident is never deleted.** If this one turns out to have been opened in error — for instance, the three "failures" were three different jobs, or the third was a duplicate log line — it is closed *as opened in error*, because the record that somebody thought this was wrong is itself worth keeping.

---

## 8. What record it has to leave behind

Every closed incident leaves a record, whatever its band. Band B is not exempt. The record has four parts:

**Timeline.** What was observed and when, **in the order it was observed, including the observations that turned out to be irrelevant.** The dead ends are part of the record, not editorial noise. This is why the incident is opened before it is understood.

**Contributing conditions.** The conditions that had to hold for this to happen — written as **conditions, not causes**, because the useful ones are usually the conditions nobody chose. For this incident, the candidates visible from the material include: that a single failure is retried automatically on the next schedule and so produces no page; that a repeat is visible only to someone reading three nights at a time; that the extract's due time and the reconciliation window can conflict on the first two working days of a month; and whatever the specific failing input turns out to be.

**Corrections.** What changed as a result, **each with a named owner. A correction with no owner is a wish and is not recorded as a correction.** The gaps flagged in this document (unnamed owning team, unnamed upstream contacts, undefined page-repeat window, undefined update cadence, undefined incident lead, ambiguous clock start, no rung above the head of platform on amber) are legitimate correction candidates — each needs an owner or it does not go in.

**Review.** The record is read by **someone who was not involved.** The reviewer's job is to find the part of the timeline that only makes sense to the people who were there.

In addition, the incident record carries the escalation lines described in §4 — rung left, rung reached, clock that expired, whether it expired unacknowledged — written as the climbs happen.

---

## 9. Handover while the incident is open

- **An incident with an open clock is never handed over silently.** The outgoing engineer walks the incoming one through it.
- **An open incident is never handed over in the notes alone.** The outgoing engineer *speaks* to the incoming one, and the notes record that they did.
- The night handover is **written as the night goes, not at the end of it**, and records which jobs completed, which failed and whether they were retried, anything left running deliberately, and anything the morning review should look at even though it did not fail — that last category being the useful one.
- **The clocks keep running across the handover.** Handing over does not reset a rung.
- The morning overnight-failure review will pick this up as a repeat regardless; hand it the four things it expects — the job, the nights involved, whether it recovered on its own, and whether anything downstream ran on partial input.

---

## 10. Consolidated gaps in the available material

These are the points where the platform's recorded material does not answer a question this incident requires. Each is stated in place above; they are gathered here so they can be raised as corrections at postmortem.

1. **The owning team for `ledger-reconcile` is not named anywhere.** Band B notification and the amber first rung both depend on it.
2. **The upstream contacts for a missing extract are not named** — the material says the manifest-missing and file-missing cases "go to different people" without saying who.
3. **The page repeat window is not quantified for any role**, so the fallback timing cannot be computed from the material.
4. **No standard update cadence is defined for any band**; the cadence is whatever the opening notice promises.
5. **The incident lead role is not defined or assigned anywhere**, though the communication rule depends entirely on it.
6. **The clock start is stated two ways** (from incident open vs. from arrival on the rung) and the two readings give different second- and third-rung climb times.
7. **The amber route has no rung above the head of platform**, yet that rung carries a two-hour clock with nowhere defined to climb to.
8. **The nightly 03:40 extract due time and the 04:00–05:30 reconciliation window conflict with the 06:00 due time on the first two working days of a month**, and nothing records how that is intended to be handled.

---

attempts.final_doc:
# order-refunds Export — Onboarding Document

**Status:** onboarding draft for a new nightly export
**Basis:** the platform's recorded operating handbook (knowledge pages). Where the handbook is silent for this export, that is stated explicitly rather than filled in.
**Operating model:** identical to `clickstream-raw`, per the *Clickstream Raw Export Runbook*.

---

## 0. How to read this document

`clickstream-raw` deliberately holds almost none of its own rules. Its runbook records only two export-specific facts — that it writes the previous day's events as hourly partitions after the collectors drain, and that it is registered under storage class **SC-4** — and defers everything else to handbook pages that are written once for every export:

| Concern | Where the rule lives |
| --- | --- |
| Job and path naming | Export Job Naming Convention |
| Where output lands, how the area is organized | Raw Zone Layout |
| Lifetime of written objects | Storage Class Register |
| Expected landing hour, lateness handling | Export Delivery Expectations |
| Safe re-run after a bad night | Export Re-run Procedure |
| Copying output off the platform | Data Egress Approval Policy |

"Operated exactly like `clickstream-raw`" therefore means: `order-refunds` inherits all six of those pages unchanged, and carries the same class-level registration (SC-4). It does **not** mean it inherits `clickstream-raw`'s upstream dependency, its landing hour, or its downstream consumers — those are per-export facts, and for `order-refunds` most of them are not yet recorded anywhere. Section 10 lists them.

---

## 1. Naming

### 1.1 The job name

The convention (*Export Job Naming Convention*) is `<subject>-<grain>`: lower case, hyphen separated, **no environment segment** — the environment is a property of the deployment, not of the job.

`order-refunds` is well formed under that convention: two lower-case hyphen-separated segments with no environment marker. It parses as subject `order`, grain `refunds`.

One thing to be aware of before the name is fixed: the handbook does not define a vocabulary of permitted `<grain>` values, so it does not settle whether `refunds` is being used as a grain in the same sense that `raw` is in `clickstream-raw`. There is already an `order-events` export in the delivery table, which suggests `order` is an established subject. The name is accepted here as given; if the owning team or the governance group wants the grain segment to describe granularity rather than subject matter, that decision has to be made **before** the first write, because renaming afterwards is expensive (§1.3).

### 1.2 The output path

Per the same convention:

- The output path **repeats the job name** — the prefix is `order-refunds`.
- After the job name come the **partition columns, in declaration order**.
- The whole thing lands inside the raw zone, whose layout is fixed for every export (§2).

So the path shape is:

```
<raw-zone bucket for the environment>/order-refunds/<partition col 1>/<partition col 2>/…
```

**Partition columns to declare.** `clickstream-raw` writes "the previous day's unaggregated event stream … as hourly partitions", and the *Export Re-run Procedure* operates on it in units of one hour within a business date. To be operable by the same procedures, `order-refunds` must be partitioned to the same grain: a **business date**, subdivided by **hour**, declared in that order (date first, then hour), so that a single hour is independently addressable and independently re-runnable.

*Gap:* the handbook nowhere records the literal column names or value formats `clickstream-raw` declares (whether the date column is `dt`, `business_date`, or similar; whether hours are `00`–`23` or zero-padded with a prefix; whether Hive-style `key=value` segments are used). Copy the declaration from the existing `clickstream-raw` job definition rather than inventing one from this document — an invented format produces a path shape that looks right and does not match the zone.

### 1.3 Renaming later

If `order-refunds` is ever renamed, the convention makes it a **two-step change**:

1. Create the new name as an **alias** and write **both** names for one full window.
2. Retire the old name only once **no consumer has read it for a week**.

A rename that skips the alias step breaks every consumer that resolves the path by string rather than by catalog lookup — "which in practice is most of them." This is the concrete reason to settle the name now.

---

## 2. Where the output lands, and how that area is organized

Per *Raw Zone Layout*:

- The raw zone holds **one bucket per environment** and **one prefix per export**. `order-refunds` gets its own prefix in each environment's bucket; the environment is expressed by which bucket is written to, never by a segment in the job name or the prefix.
- Underneath the prefix, partitions are laid out by the export's **declared partition columns in declaration order**, so the same path shape works for every export in the zone.
- **Nothing writes outside its own prefix.** `order-refunds` must not write into `order-events`, `clickstream-raw`, or any other export's area, and nothing else may write into `order-refunds`.
- A job that needs `order-refunds` output **reads it in place**. It must not copy it under a second prefix: that "produces two datasets that drift apart and are both believed."
- **Do not discover the prefix by listing the bucket.** The zone is not browsable by hand at any useful scale — on the larger exports a listing takes minutes and returns tens of thousands of keys. Use the **catalog entry** for `order-refunds` to find its prefix. This makes registering a catalog entry for the new export a hard prerequisite of onboarding, not a nicety.

*Gap:* the handbook does not record the literal bucket names per environment, or how many environments exist. Take those from the existing zone configuration.

### 2.1 File layout after the write

Per *Partition Compaction Notes*, a partition written by an export lands as **many small files, one per writer**. Compaction rewrites them into a few large files once the file count crosses a trigger that is **set per dataset and defaults to two hundred files**. Two consequences for `order-refunds`:

- A compaction trigger will be applied at the default of 200 files unless the owning team sets one deliberately. Decide whether the default suits this export's writer count.
- **Compaction changes the layout and nothing else.** The partition keeps its **original write date**, because that date is a property of the data, not of the last time the bytes were touched, and every lifecycle decision downstream is made against the original date. Compaction therefore never extends the life of an `order-refunds` partition (§3).
- Compaction runs opportunistically inside the maintenance window (00:45–02:00 per the *Nightly Batch Window Calendar*) and is **safe to skip**; a skipped partition is simply compacted the following night. An uncompacted `order-refunds` partition in the morning is not an incident.

---

## 3. Storage registration and how long the output lives

### 3.1 The registration

`clickstream-raw` is registered under **storage class SC-4**. Operated identically, `order-refunds` is registered under **SC-4** as well.

From the *Storage Class Register*:

| Class | Tier | Purge window |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SC-1 | hot | 7 days |
| SC-2 | hot | 30 days |
| SC-3 | warm | 45 days |
| SC-4 | **warm** | **62 days** |
| SC-5 | cold | 400 days |
| SC-6 | archive | held indefinitely |

So `order-refunds` partitions sit on the **warm** tier and are purged **62 days** after their write date.

### 3.2 What the class does and does not allow

- **The class fixes both the tier and the lifetime. Nothing else sets a lifetime.** The `order-refunds` job must set no retention of its own — `clickstream-raw` explicitly "sets no lifetime of its own", and the register states flatly that "a job that wants its output kept longer is asking to be reclassified."
- The purge **runs daily** and removes **whole objects** once their write date is older than the window. **An object is never partially removed**, so a window boundary falling inside an object keeps the whole object until the next boundary. Expect the effective retention of any given `order-refunds` object to be 62 days *or slightly more*, never less.
- **A partition is the unit** of writing and purging (*Platform Glossary*). Nothing is written or removed in units smaller than a partition.

### 3.3 If 62 days is wrong for refunds

Any request to keep `order-refunds` partitions longer is a **reclassification request**, not a change to this job, and not a per-dataset override. Per the register:

- Reclassification requests are **reviewed monthly**.
- A move **up** the tiers (cold→warm, warm→hot) needs a **stated reason for the extra cost**.
- A move **down** needs **confirmation from the owning team that nothing reads the older partitions**.
- A class is **never changed in place for a single dataset without updating the register**, because "the purge reads the register and not the request." A change agreed in a ticket but not written into the register will not take effect.

*Judgment to make before go-live:* refund data may carry a finance or audit retention obligation that 62 days does not satisfy. The handbook does not say whether it does. If a consumer of `order-refunds` is **obliged to reproduce its contents on demand**, that is the trigger for the **regulated tier** (*Regulated Tier Operating Rules*), which is assigned by the **data governance group**, reviewed annually, and carries a retention floor plus quarterly access review and producer attestation. Note that those rules are written for *streams*; the handbook does not state whether or how the regulated tier applies to a raw-zone export. Put the question to the governance group during onboarding rather than assuming SC-4 discharges it.

---

## 4. When it is expected to land

### 4.1 The expectation

*Export Delivery Expectations* records an expected landing hour per export, **measured at the moment the last partition is written** — not when the job starts:

| Export | Expected by |
| --- | --- |
| clickstream-raw | 02:00 |
| order-events | 02:30 |
| ledger-extract | 03:40 |

**`order-refunds` has no entry in this table.** This is the single largest gap in this onboarding, and it cannot be filled by copying `clickstream-raw`: the expected hour is a per-export fact that depends on when the export's upstream is ready and what reads it downstream, and `order-refunds` shares neither with `clickstream-raw`.

**Action:** the owning team proposes an expected hour and the row is added to *Export Delivery Expectations* before the first production night. Until that row exists, the export cannot be late in any measurable sense, so none of §4.2 has anything to fire on — the job would run unmonitored.

Two constraints to inform the proposed hour:

- The *Nightly Batch Window Calendar* gives the **raw exports** window as **23:15–00:45**, between collector drain (22:00–23:15) and maintenance/vacuum (00:45–02:00), with aggregation from 02:00 and reconciliation from 04:00. `order-refunds` belongs to the raw-exports family and should run in that window.
- The expected *landing hour* is a separate figure from the *window*, and sits later than it in every recorded case (`clickstream-raw` runs in a window closing at 00:45 but is expected by 02:00). So the expected hour is a delivery commitment with headroom, not the window end. Propose it deliberately.

If `order-refunds` cannot fit the 23:15–00:45 window, moving a window is a **scheduling change, not a job change**: the request goes to the platform group with the reason and the earliest night it can take effect. A job that overruns its window is not killed, but the window behind it starts late and **the delay accumulates across the night**. Any move that pushes a window past 05:30 needs the **aggregation owner's agreement**, because the morning reports read what aggregation writes.

### 4.2 Lateness, and what happens when it is repeated

- **Lateness is counted in whole hours past the expected time** and is **reported in the morning run review**.
- **An export that is late three mornings in a row is raised with its owning team** — "because at that point the expectation is wrong or the job is." That is the recorded consequence of repeated lateness, and it applies to `order-refunds` unchanged once its row exists. Note the disposition: repeated lateness is treated as a question about whether the *expectation* is correct, as much as about the job. The remedy may legitimately be a revised expected hour rather than a code fix.
- The morning review that catches this (*Overnight Failure Review*) **reads three nights at a time rather than one**, precisely so a repeat is visible: "a job that failed once is noise; the same job failing on consecutive nights is the thing the review exists to notice." The review is **a reading, not a repair** — it hands anything needing a fix to the owning team.
- For each failure the review hands on: the job, the nights involved, whether it recovered on its own, and **whether anything downstream ran on partial input**. The last is flagged as the one that gets missed, "because a job that succeeded on incomplete input leaves no failure anywhere." For `order-refunds`, whichever jobs are wired to read it must be listed so this question can actually be answered (§10).
- The overnight shift's *Night Shift Handover Notes* are written **as the night goes**, and record which jobs completed, which failed and whether they were retried, anything left running deliberately, and **anything the morning review should look at even though it did not fail**. An `order-refunds` run that completes while doing something odd is invisible unless it is written down.

### 4.3 A missing drop overnight

Vocabulary (*Platform Glossary*): a **drop** is one scheduled delivery of an export; a **missing drop** did not arrive, a **late drop** arrived outside its window. Also: **a job fails when it cannot complete; a job reports a problem when it completes and does not like what it saw.** These "are worked by different people on different clocks, and conflating them is the reason most overnight pages reach the wrong person." Wire and triage `order-refunds` alarms with that distinction explicit.

`clickstream-raw`'s runbook says a missing hourly partition is "almost always a collector that has not drained rather than an export failure" — check upstream lag first, then re-run the single hour. The *structure* of that advice transfers: **for `order-refunds`, check upstream readiness before concluding the export failed.** The *content* does not — `order-refunds` does not read the event collectors, and its upstream is not recorded anywhere (§10). The `clickstream-raw` drain signal, the two-minute lag metric, the restart-don't-hand-drain rule, and the mark-the-hour-as-held fallback in the *Event Collector Drain Runbook* are all specific to the collectors and must **not** be applied to `order-refunds` by analogy. The equivalent upstream check has to be written down by the owning team.

### 4.4 If it becomes an incident

The handbook does **not** say that a late export automatically opens an incident — the recorded path for lateness is the morning review and, after three consecutive mornings, the owning team. If a night's failure does warrant an incident, these apply as they do to any job:

- **Severity bands** (*Incident Severity Bands*) are a statement about **consequence, not effort**: **Band A** = customer-visible loss of service or a defect that has already produced an incorrect external figure; **Band B** = an internal control that has stopped proving what it exists to prove, no external figure yet affected; **Band C** = degradation with a known workaround already in place; **Band D** = a defect with no consequence before the next working day. A missed `order-refunds` drop that has not yet reached an external figure lands at Band B or below on the recorded definitions; a refund figure already published wrong would be Band A. The band is assigned when the incident is opened.
- **Routes** (*Escalation Ladders*): Band A → **red**, Band B → **amber**, Bands C and D → **standard**. An incident starts at the first rung and climbs one rung at a time; skipping a rung is allowed only when the person on it is the one escalating.
  - Red: owning team's shift lead → platform duty manager → head of platform → executive on call.
  - Amber: owning team's shift lead → platform duty manager → head of platform.
  - Standard: owning team's shift lead → owning team's manager, **during working hours only**.
- **Clocks** (*Duty Manager Response Matrix*) — the longest an incident may sit on a rung before it must reach the next:

  | Route | First rung | Second rung | Third rung |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Red | 5 minutes | 10 minutes | 30 minutes |
  | Amber | 20 minutes | 25 minutes | 2 hours |
  | Standard | 4 hours | next working day | next working day |

  A clock **starts when the incident is opened, not when it is acknowledged**, and runs across shift handovers. An expired unacknowledged clock **climbs on its own**. Between **22:00 and 06:00 the standard route's clocks are doubled** (the rung below is on a pager, not at a desk); red and amber run to the same clocks at every hour. Every climb writes a line to the incident record: the rung left, the rung reached, the clock that expired, and whether it expired unacknowledged. Since `order-refunds` runs overnight, the doubled standard clock is the one that will usually apply.
- **Channels** (*Paging Channel Directory*): shift lead — pager app, fallback phone; duty manager — phone, fallback pager app; head of platform — phone, fallback assistant's phone; executive on call — phone, no fallback. A page unacknowledged on the primary repeats on the fallback; unacknowledged on both, the role is treated as unreachable and **the sender moves on rather than waiting**.
- An **open incident is never handed over in the handover notes alone** — the outgoing engineer speaks to the incoming one, and the notes record that they did.

---

## 5. Re-running after a bad night

*Export Re-run Procedure* applies to `order-refunds` unchanged. `clickstream-raw`'s runbook confirms this is the intended relationship: the safe way to re-run "is written up once for every export (and applies here unchanged)."

**The governing property: a re-run replaces what it writes, and exports here are idempotent per partition.** Re-running one hour rewrites that hour and leaves the rest of the night alone. This is why the hourly partition declaration in §1.2 matters operationally — it is what makes a surgical re-run possible.

### 5.1 Single hour — the usual case

Re-run the single affected hour, then **tell the downstream jobs that read it**. Do not re-run the whole night for one bad hour.

Note the shape of the downstream obligation, using `clickstream-raw`'s recorded example: the export is re-run **per hour**, but its downstream consumer (*Sessionization Job Runbook*) is idempotent **per business date** and needs a re-run of **the whole business date, not of the hour**. A late partition is handled by re-running the date once the partition has landed — **never by patching the output**. The equivalent statement for `order-refunds` — which consumers exist, and what unit each must be re-run in — is not recorded and must be written down as part of onboarding (§10). Without it, step "tell the downstream jobs" has no addressee.

### 5.2 Whole night — narrow and conditional

A whole-night re-run is **only** for the case where the export ran against the **wrong business date**. It writes every hour again and is safe, but there is a trap:

> **It does not remove the partitions written under the wrong date.** Those are removed **by hand**, and **until they are, both dates look complete.**

For `order-refunds` this is the highest-consequence failure mode in the whole document: refund data present under two business dates, both appearing complete, silently double-counted by anything that reads a date range. Treat manual removal of the wrong-date partitions as a mandatory, verified step of a whole-night re-run, not a follow-up.

### 5.3 What a re-run does not do

**A re-run never changes an object's original write date, so it does not extend anything's life in the raw zone.** Combined with §3, this means a re-run of a partition that is already 60 days old buys **two days**, not another 62 — it will be purged on the original write date's schedule. The same principle applies to compaction (§2.1). Anything that needs an old `order-refunds` partition preserved needs reclassification (§3.3), not a re-run.

---

## 6. If any output is ever copied outside the platform

*Data Egress Approval Policy* governs this, and `clickstream-raw`'s runbook explicitly routes here: anything leaving the platform boundary, **including a copy of these partitions to a partner bucket**, is governed separately.

### 6.1 What counts

> **Any route that writes platform data to a destination the platform does not operate is an egress, whether it runs once or nightly.**

There is no ad-hoc exemption. A one-off manual copy of a single `order-refunds` partition to a partner or vendor destination is an egress on exactly the same terms as a scheduled nightly feed. This is worth stating plainly for a refunds dataset, which is the kind of data a finance, payments, or partner team is likely to ask for by hand.

Note also that even *inside* the platform, copying `order-refunds` output under a second raw-zone prefix is prohibited by *Raw Zone Layout* (§2) — consumers read it in place.

### 6.2 What approval requires

Before approval, an egress route needs all three:

1. a **named recipient**,
2. a **stated purpose**,
3. an **end date**.

**Approval sits with the data governance group** — not the owning team, not the duty manager.

- **A route without an end date is not approved.** There is no perpetual egress.
- **A route whose end date has passed is disabled automatically rather than reviewed**, and **re-enabling it is a new request** — a fresh recipient, purpose, and end date, and fresh governance approval. Plan renewals ahead of the end date; expiry is not a prompt to discuss, it is a stop.

### 6.3 What an approved route must record

Every approved route records, **per run**, **what it sent and how much of it**. The policy is emphatic about why:

> "The record is the point of the approval: an egress nobody can describe afterwards is indistinguishable from one that was never approved."

Any `order-refunds` egress must therefore emit a per-run record of content and volume from day one. A route that copies data correctly but keeps no per-run record has not satisfied the policy.

*Gap:* the handbook does not record where these per-run egress records are stored, in what format, or how long they are kept. Confirm with the data governance group when the route is proposed. It also does not state whether the destination-side copy inherits the SC-4 purge window; on the plain reading it does not, since the class register governs what the platform writes — settle this with governance as part of the approval.

---

## 7. Changing the export once it is live

Not asked directly, but it determines what onboarding must set up now.

*Change Class Reference*: every interface the platform publishes carries a **change class**, and the class decides the paperwork and the notice — a change is planned from its class, not its size.

- **CC-1 local** — no published interface changes; owning team signs off, no notice owed.
- **CC-2 additive** — compatible addition; owning team signs off, **2 business days** notice.
- **CC-3 governed** — interface whose consumers carry an obligation of their own; **governance group** signs off, **9 business days** notice.
- **CC-4 breaking** — invalidates a published contract; governance signs off, **a full quarter** of notice, old contract runs in parallel until the last consumer has moved.
- **CC-5 emergency** — applied ahead of its notice because leaving the defect in place is worse; **duty manager** signs off, notice reconstructed afterwards with the reason recorded.

Notice is counted in **business days from announcement to the change window opening, excluding the announcement day**; a notice period that would end inside a change freeze runs to **the first business day after the freeze lifts**.

Announcements (*Change Announcement Channels*) go to **three places at once**: the platform mailing list, the platform channel, and **the registry entry for the interface being changed** — the registry entry is **authoritative**, because it is the only channel a consumer onboarded after the announcement will still see. An announcement contains **what is changing, the window it will be applied in, who signed it off, and how a consumer says it is not ready** — and deliberately **not** a justification.

*Gap:* the handbook assigns change classes to *interfaces* and states that every **regulated-tier stream** is CC-3, but it does not record what class a raw-zone export path carries by default, nor what class *creating* a new export falls under. Have the class for the `order-refunds` output path assigned at onboarding, and record it on the registry entry — otherwise the first schema change to this export will have no defensible notice period. Note that a later rename is a change to a published path and so carries both a class obligation here *and* the alias procedure in §1.3.

---

## 8. Onboarding checklist

Ordered, with the owner where the handbook names one.

**Before the first write**

1. Confirm the job name `order-refunds` against the `<subject>-<grain>` convention and settle the grain-segment question in §1.1. *Owning team.*
2. Copy the **partition column declaration** (business date, then hour) verbatim from the `clickstream-raw` job definition; do not reconstruct it. *Owning team.*
3. Create the `order-refunds` **prefix** in the raw-zone bucket for **each environment**; confirm no other export writes into it and it writes into no other. *Owning team.*
4. Register **storage class SC-4** in the *Storage Class Register* for this dataset — warm tier, 62-day purge. Confirm the job itself sets **no** lifetime of its own. *Owning team + register owner.*
5. Put the regulated-tier / retention question (§3.3) to the **data governance group** and record the answer. *Governance group.*
6. Create the **catalog entry** for `order-refunds` recording its prefix — required, because the zone is not browsable by hand and consumers are expected to resolve the prefix by catalog lookup. *Owning team.*
7. Set the **compaction trigger**, or accept the 200-file default deliberately. *Owning team.*
8. Assign a **change class** to the output path and record it on the registry entry (§7). *Governance group.*

**Before the first production night**

9. Claim a slot in the **23:15–00:45 raw exports window**, or request a window move via the platform group with reason and earliest effective night. *Platform group.*
10. Propose an **expected landing hour** and add the `order-refunds` row to *Export Delivery Expectations*. Without this row the export is unmonitored. *Owning team.*
11. Write down the **upstream readiness check** — what `order-refunds` waits on, how "ready" is signalled, and what to check first when a partition is missing (§4.3). *Owning team.*
12. Record the **owning team, shift lead, and manager** so the escalation rungs in §4.4 resolve to real people. *Owning team.*
13. List the **downstream consumers** and, for each, the unit it must be re-run in (hour vs. business date), so §5.1's "tell the downstream jobs" has an addressee. *Owning team.*
14. Wire alarms that distinguish **failing** from **reporting a problem** (§4.3). *Owning team.*
15. Confirm the export appears in the **night shift handover** template and in the **morning failure review**'s three-night reading. *On-call rotation.*

**Only if output will leave the platform**

16. Submit the egress request with **named recipient, stated purpose, and end date** to the **data governance group**; build the **per-run record of what was sent and how much** before the first run; diarise the end date, since expiry disables the route automatically and re-enabling is a new request. *Governance group + owning team.*

---

## 9. What this export does *not* inherit from `clickstream-raw`

Stated explicitly, because copying these would be wrong:

- **The collector drain dependency.** The *Event Collector Drain Runbook* — the drain signal, the five-minute cycle, the two-minute lag metric, restart-don't-hand-drain, mark-the-hour-as-held — is specific to the event collectors that feed `clickstream-raw`. None of it is known to apply to `order-refunds`.
- **The 02:00 landing hour.** Per-export, and per *Export Delivery Expectations*, must be set for `order-refunds` on its own merits.
- **The sessionization consumer**, its six-hour lookback, its per-business-date idempotency, and its sessions-span-midnight rule. That is a `clickstream-raw` consumer.
- **The clickstream schema.** The envelope/properties-map structure, the device-vs-account identity fields, and the pre-upgrade local-time timestamp gap in *Clickstream Schema Notes* describe clickstream records. `order-refunds` has no schema notes page; one should be written to the same standard.

---

## 10. Open items — where the recorded material is silent

Every item below is a genuine gap in the platform's records, not an omission from this document. None can be filled by analogy with `clickstream-raw`.

| # | Unrecorded | Consequence if left open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Expected landing hour** for `order-refunds` | No row in *Export Delivery Expectations* → lateness is unmeasurable, the three-consecutive-mornings escalation never fires, the export runs unmonitored |
| 2 | **Owning team**, its shift lead and manager | The first rung of every escalation route is undefined; the three-late-mornings escalation has no recipient |
| 3 | **Upstream source and readiness signal** | No first check when a partition is missing; the `clickstream-raw` collector guidance does not transfer |
| 4 | **Downstream consumers** and the re-run unit each needs | §5.1 cannot be completed; the failure review cannot answer "did anything run on partial input?" |
| 5 | **Literal partition column names and value formats** | Path shape may look correct and not match the zone; take from the `clickstream-raw` job definition |
| 6 | **Raw-zone bucket names per environment**, and how many environments | Prefix cannot be created from this document alone |
| 7 | **Whether refund data carries a retention obligation beyond SC-4's 62 days**, and whether the regulated tier applies to exports at all (its rules are written for streams) | Data may be purged before an audit or finance obligation is met; reclassification is reviewed only monthly, so a late discovery costs weeks |
| 8 | **Change class for a raw-zone export path**, and the class covering *creation* of a new export | First schema change to `order-refunds` has no defensible notice period |
| 9 | **Schema notes** for `order-refunds` (record structure, identity fields, money fields and their units, known gaps) | Consumers reconstruct the schema by inspection; `clickstream-raw` has such a page and this export does not |
| 10 | **Where per-run egress records are stored, in what format, and for how long**; whether an egressed copy inherits any purge window | An egress route can be built that satisfies the letter of approval and still cannot describe itself afterwards |

Items 1–4 are blocking for a first production night. Items 5–6 are blocking for a first write. Items 7–10 are blocking only for the situations they describe, but 7 should be settled early because reclassification is on a monthly review cycle.
